title: Tensor Network Solvers for Ultra-large Tight-binding Hamiltonians: Algorithms and Applications
authors: Tiago V. C. Antão, Anouar Moustaj, Yitao Sun, Jose L. Lado
abstract: Understanding quantum materials at meso and even macroscopic scales requires tight-binding calculations on system sizes where explicit matrix representations become prohibitively costly. This represents a major bottleneck to rationalize phenomena in moiré and super-moiré heterostructures and quasicrystals. Here, we present a unified tensor-network methodology to solve tight-binding problems at exceptionally large scales, by mapping a system of $N = 2^L$ sites onto a many-body problem of $L$ pseudospin sites, which is subsequently solved with tensor network algorithms. For Hamiltonians with compressible real-space structure, the tensor network bond dimension remains modest, typically of order a few tens, independent of $N$.Tensor network representations of arbitrary hopping functions including long-range, spatially modulated, and twisted-layer couplings are built with quantics tensor cross interpolation, and all physical observables are evaluated entirely with tensor network algebra without explicit matrix storage or diagonalization. We demonstrate applications to spectral functions, momentum-space spectra via the tensor-network quantum Fourier transform, real-space topological invariants, real-time dynamics, correlation induced symmetry breaking with self-consistent mean-field calculations, non-Hermitian phenomena, and excitonic many-body physics. Our methodology enables routinely solving systems with billions of sites, by leveraging the tensor network compressibility of real-space structures, and establishing a flexible framework to study quantum matter at ultra-large length scales. The methodology is implemented in the open-source Julia package TensorBinding.jl.
summary: The paper introduces an advanced tensor network framework to solve tight-binding Hamiltonians on systems of unprecedented size. By mapping large lattices onto efficient pseudospin chains, it allows routine calculation of complex observables like spectral functions and topological invariants for quantum materials at the mesoscopic scale. This methodology overcomes severe memory bottlenecks associated with simulating ultra-large quantum systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is simulating quantum materials on systems so large (billions of sites) that explicit matrix representations for tight-binding Hamiltonians become computationally prohibitive.
main_result: The authors present a unified tensor-network methodology capable of solving these ultra-large scale problems by mapping the system onto a manageable pseudospin chain, keeping memory scaling logarithmic with system size.
method: They utilize Matrix Product Operators (MPO) and Tensor Network algorithms, combined with the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM), to evaluate observables without explicit diagonalization or storage of massive matrices.
model_or_system: The method applies to tight-binding Hamiltonians on various lattices, including moiré/super-moiré heterostructures and quasicrystals. It handles complex physics like non-Hermiticity, correlation effects (Hubbard model), and excitonic binding.
key_observables: Spectral functions $A(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$, real-space topological invariants (Chern marker), local density of states (LDOS), time-dependent currents, and exciton spectral weight.
important_parameters: System sizes up to billions of sites; bond dimension ($\chi$) remaining modest (tens) for compressible structures; Chebyshev polynomial order ($N_{	ext{cheb}}$).
main_assumptions: The efficiency relies heavily on the tensor network compressibility inherent in the real-space structure, and spectral calculations are approximations via KPM.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping from large real-space lattices to 1D pseudospin chains (Fig. 2), the calculation of various observables like spectral functions and topological markers using MPO representations (Figs. 1, 6, 7, 10).
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops algorithms for encoding Hamiltonians ($\hat{H}$) as MPOs, then details specialized pathways to compute key quantities: spectral functions via KPM, topological invariants via position operators, and time evolution/correlations using MPO-MPO products.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, scalable numerical toolkit for simulating complex quantum matter phenomena (like moiré physics or correlated states) that are typically restricted to small system sizes by conventional diagonalization methods.
